description: From the summer of 1942 to February 1943, Germans and Soviets killed each other in the ruins of a city on the Volga. Stalingrad became the turning point of the Second World War.

hero.hook: In the ruins of one city, the army everyone called invincible broke for good.

blocks.text: From the summer of **1942** to **February 2, 1943**, the world watched a strip of ruins on the **Volga**, one of the great rivers of Russia. At **Stalingrad** (today Volgograd), the German army ran into a Soviet defense ready for any sacrifice.
With more than **a million** dead, it is the deadliest battle in history, and the point where the Second World War tipped over.

After failing to take Moscow in 1941, Hitler launched [[Case Blue]], a summer offensive toward the south. The target: the oil of the **Caucasus**. **Stalingrad**, a rail and river hub on the Volga, was at first only a secondary objective. Then the symbol took over: capturing the city that carried **Stalin**'s name became an obsession.

blocks.caption: Stalingrad in ruins: an urban battlefield without mercy

blocks.text: Hitler was so sure of winning that he is said to have had invitations printed for a victory banquet at the Hotel Lux in Stalingrad.

The German **6th Army**, commanded by General [[Friedrich Paulus]], was diverted toward the city. In August 1942 the bombing raids of the [[Luftwaffe]], the German air force, left a landscape of craters, perfect for the Soviet defense.

sections.title: Hitler goes after the oil of the south

blocks.text: The Soviet general **Vasily Chuikov** imposed a simple tactic: stay within **30 meters** of the enemy. German guns and aircraft could then not strike without killing their own men. The Germans called it **Rattenkrieg**, the “war of the rats”: the fighting went on in cellars, in sewers, in gutted buildings.

**Pavlov's House**, a single building held by a handful of soldiers, held out for **58 days**. In the **Dzerzhinsky** factory, workers built tanks under the bombs and drove them straight to the front. Stalin's **Order 227** summed up the instruction: **“Not one step back.”**

While Paulus wore himself out in the rubble, the Soviet marshal **Georgy Zhukov** prepared [[Operation Uranus]]. The German flanks, held by poorly equipped allies (Romanians, Italians, Hungarians), gave way. On **November 19, 1942**, the pincers closed: about **300,000** men were surrounded.
The Soviets played the ticking of a clock over loudspeakers, then a message: one German soldier was dying every **7 seconds** in the USSR.
Hitler forbade any breakout. [[Hermann Göring]], head of the Luftwaffe, promised to supply the army by air. He failed. Hunger, typhus, **-30°C**: the “cauldron” became a death trap.

sections.title: The pincers that closed the trap

blocks.text: On **January 30, 1943**, Hitler made Paulus a **field marshal**, the highest rank, to push him to die rather than surrender. Paulus capitulated on **February 2**. Of the 300,000 men encircled, **91,000** went into captivity. For the first time, Nazi propaganda had to admit a total defeat. The army everyone called invincible had been broken.

blocks.text: **Stalingrad** (**1942-1943**) destroyed the German 6th Army and broke the myth of Nazi invincibility, in the deadliest battle in history.
